title: fix(salience): exclude briefings/* from their own Brain Pulse
body:
## Problem

The daily briefing writes its output back into the vault, where it re-ingests as `briefings/<date>`. On the next run that freshly-touched page tops `getRecentSalience()` (the Brain Pulse), so the briefing perpetually surfaces **itself** as the most salient recent activity — pure self-reference with no real signal. Over time the Pulse becomes a list of past briefings instead of the underlying knowledge that changed.

## Fix

Exclude `briefings/%` slugs from `getRecentSalience()` in both engines (`PostgresEngine`, `PGLiteEngine`), *unless* the caller explicitly scopes the query to the `briefings/` prefix (in which case they asked for them). The suppression is a single `AND p.slug NOT LIKE 'briefings/%'` clause gated on the requested `slugPrefix`.

## Tests

Adds PGLite E2E coverage in `test/e2e/salience-pglite.test.ts`:
- default query hides `briefings/*` slugs
- explicit `slugPrefix='briefings/'` still returns them

`bun test test/e2e/salience-pglite.test.ts` passes (7 tests).

title: feat(engine): opt-in Postgres RLS source-scope binding
body:
## What this does

Adds opt-in [Postgres Row-Level Security](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-rowsecurity.html) scope binding to the engine's source-scoped read methods. When the environment variable `GBRAIN_RLS_SCOPE_BINDING=1` is set, every source-scoped read is wrapped in a transaction that sets a session variable `app.scopes` from the caller's allowed sources. A matching RLS policy on `pages` (and other source-scoped tables) then filters rows at the SQL layer — even when the application code path doesn't apply the source filter itself.

Default behavior is **unchanged**: with the env var unset, `withScopedReadTransaction` is effectively pass-through (one tx round-trip per read, no semantic change). Operators who don't want this see zero behavior difference on upgrade.

## Why

Defense in depth. Today the engine enforces source scope at the application layer — every read method has to remember to apply the filter. If any code path drifts (the comment in `sourceScopeOpts` calls out "drift between sites is the bug class"), the only safety net is the next code review. RLS gives the database itself a vote: a row's `source_id` not in the caller's grant set never reaches the network buffer.

This was caught when a federated OAuth client read past its grant due to a single op handler that dropped the federated array. The fix was already addressed at the app layer by #2200 (federated_read scope reaches by-slug reads in v0.42.46.0). This PR is the orthogonal defense-in-depth layer that catches the next instance of that bug class before it ships.

## How it works (the helper)

`withScopedReadTransaction(sourceIds?, sourceId?, callback)`:
1. Always opens a transaction. (Lets nested `SET LOCAL` calls in search methods scope cleanly; avoids `tx.begin` not being callable inside a postgres.js transaction handle.)
2. When `GBRAIN_RLS_SCOPE_BINDING=1`, emits `SELECT set_config('app.scopes', $1, true)` with `$1` derived from `sourceIds.join(',') || sourceId || '*'`. The `true` makes it transaction-local (equivalent to `SET LOCAL` but parameterised — `SET LOCAL` itself doesn't accept bound params, so `set_config()` is the right tool).
3. Calls back with the transaction handle.
4. When the env var is off: same wrap, no `set_config` emit. The transaction is the no-op overhead (~ms per read).

## Recommended RLS policy

For operators who turn this on:

```sql
ALTER TABLE pages ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY pages_scope_filter ON pages
  USING (current_setting('app.scopes', true) = '*'
         OR source_id = ANY(string_to_array(current_setting('app.scopes', true), ',')));

-- For admin / autopilot / cycle connections that shouldn't be source-scoped:
ALTER ROLE <runtime-role> SET app.scopes = '*';
```

The `string_to_array` form handles a single source as well as the comma-separated federated set.

## Layered with #2200 (federated by-slug reads)

This PR sits on top of upstream HEAD which already includes v0.42.46.0 (federated `sourceIds[]` scope on by-slug secondary reads). The two layers compose cleanly:

- **App-layer (existing, v0.42.46.0)**: `getPage` / `getLinks` / `getBacklinks` filter rows with `AND source_id = ANY(${sourceIds}::text[])`.
- **SQL-layer (this PR, opt-in)**: same operations also wrap in `withScopedReadTransaction(sourceIds, sourceId, ...)` so the RLS policy enforces from below.

The three methods touched by both #2200 and this PR's commit `feat(postgres-engine): wrap remaining 16 source-scoped methods` keep both layers active.

## Commits

5 logical commits — left separate for review:

1. `feat(postgres-engine): opt-in RLS scope binding via SET LOCAL app.scopes` — adds the helper, defaulted off.
2. `fix(postgres-engine): use set_config() instead of SET LOCAL for parameterised scope binding` — small follow-up; `SET LOCAL` doesn't accept bound params.
3. `feat(postgres-engine): wrap remaining 16 source-scoped methods with withScopedReadTransaction` — the bulk of the wrap.
4. `fix(postgres-engine): flatten nested tx.begin in search methods + always-open wrap` — handles the postgres.js gotcha that transaction handles expose `.savepoint()` not `.begin()`.
5. `fix(postgres-engine): cast withScopedReadTransaction return to T` — typecheck fixup (`UnwrapPromiseArray<T>` → `T`).

Happy to squash on request.

## Compatibility

- **`GBRAIN_RLS_SCOPE_BINDING` unset / `0`**: helper is pass-through (one extra tx round-trip per read). No RLS policy required. **Default behavior for every existing operator.**
- **`GBRAIN_RLS_SCOPE_BINDING=1`** without an RLS policy on `pages`: still works — `set_config` is called but no policy enforces the value. Safe to enable in isolation before the policy is created.
- **`GBRAIN_RLS_SCOPE_BINDING=1`** + policy created: full defense-in-depth.

## Tests

`bun run verify` — all 30 checks pass (typecheck, privacy, jsonb, progress, test-isolation, wasm, admin-build, resolver, etc.) on the rebased branch against current upstream HEAD.

Manual verification on a Postgres 16 install with the policy applied: opt-in enabled, a federated OAuth client (`allowed_sources={a,b,c,d,e,f}`) confirmed to read across all granted sources via `query` / `get_page` / `list_pages`. A subject-scoped token (`allowed_sources={a}`) confirmed unable to read pages from `b` even when the operation handler is called with `source_id=b` — the RLS policy blocks the row return.

Happy to iterate on any of the above, or split into smaller PRs if you'd prefer (e.g. helper + getPage wrap first, then the remaining 15 wraps as a follow-up).



## Related work

Adjacent and complementary efforts in the same RLS defense-in-depth thread:

- **#2457** — `fix(security): views enforce caller RLS via security_invoker` (open). Flips gbrain's views from default `security_definer` to `security_invoker`, so views enforce the caller's RLS rather than the view owner's. Composes naturally with this PR: their fix ensures policies fire through views; this PR supplies the session-scoped value (`app.scopes`) those policies key off. Two layers, one posture.
- **#2454** — `tag-filtered query/search for profile-scoped retrieval` (open). Read-side scoping at the operations layer; this PR is the SQL-layer enforcement that makes that scoping load-bearing rather than advisory.
- **#2239** / **#2200** — merged app-layer fix (`v0.42.46.0`) where federated `sourceIds[]` reach by-slug reads. This PR is the orthogonal SQL-layer defense to the same threat class — drift in any single operation handler is caught at the database boundary instead of the next review.
- **#612** — `v0.26.8 feat(migration): v35 auto-RLS event trigger — new tables always secure`. Precedent for accepting opt-in RLS infrastructure that's a no-op for the unrestricted case and load-bearing for managed-Postgres deployments. Same shape as the env-var gate proposed here.
- **#1403** — `v0.41.3.0 fix(security/mcp): OAuth CORS lockdown + pre-register without DCR + validator surface`. Same defense-in-depth flavour at the MCP boundary; this PR extends the posture inward to the SQL row layer.

title: Feature: Life Chronicle — temporal timeline + thought diary + dynamic per-entity ontology
body:
## Feature: Life Chronicle — a temporal + introspective layer for gbrain

### Summary

gbrain today is an excellent **document store with semantic + structured retrieval** (pages + typed `frontmatter JSONB` + embeddings + SQL). What it lacks is a layer that turns a pile of pages into a **model of a subject over time**.

This proposes a **Life Chronicle**: three interlocking objects built entirely on existing gbrain primitives —

1. **Daily Timeline** — auto-assembled events (`when · where · who · what`), each backlinking to the rich page that holds the depth.
2. **Thought Diary** — timestamped, low-friction interiority, backlinked to events/entities; the raw material for cross-time pattern detection.
3. **Dynamic per-entity ontology** — an open-world, sourced, confidence-weighted property bag on each entity page, where salient dimensions *emerge from observation* instead of fitting a fixed schema.

The pages remain the **depth**. The Life Chronicle is the **structure over the depth**. It is both a retrieval/introspection tool for the human and a context substrate for agents.

### Motivation

Concrete failure that motivated this: a single day's activity was captured across several rich meeting pages, but the **chronological spine** — the order of events, who was where, what came before what — was scattered across those pages. An agent reconstructing the day repeatedly got the sequence wrong (e.g. conflating a "before" event with an "after" event, or mislocating who was present at which event), because **a meeting page is great at depth and bad at sequence**. There was no object whose job is "the timeline."

Two distinct gaps fall out of that:
- Agents can't reliably answer *"what was happening the week of X?"* or *"when did the subject last interact with entity Y?"* — there's no temporal index, only a keyword/semantic one.
- There's no place for *interiority over time* — reactions, uncertainty, evolving takes — so longitudinal patterns ("every time situation Z came up, the reaction was W") must be re-derived from scratch each session instead of being queryable.

### Design

#### Object 1 — Event (timeline atom)

One Event = one page (`type: event`) with typed frontmatter + a one-clause summary that links out. Cheap; a day produces a handful.

```yaml
---
type: event
t_start: 2026-01-15T16:30:00-08:00   # ISO; date-only allowed, with t_approx: true
t_end:   2026-01-15T19:00:00-08:00   # optional
place:
  name: "Example Venue"
  area: "Example District"
  geo: [37.7587, -122.4112]          # optional
people: [person-a, person-b]          # refs to entity pages
kind: meeting                         # meeting|call|meal|solo|travel|work|... (open vocab)
mood: [focused]                       # optional, light affect tags
source: transcription                 # transcription|calendar|message|manual|inferred
confidence: high                      # high|med|low (for inferred/fuzzy timing)
links:
  - meetings/2026-01-15-example.md    # the depth page
summary: "Project sync — scope cut agreed, follow-up next week."
---
```

#### Object 2 — Diary entry (introspective atom)

```yaml
---
type: diary
t: 2026-01-16T08:10:00-08:00
people: [person-a]
events: [life/events/2026-01-15-002-example]   # what it reflects on
themes: [decision-making, uncertainty]
affect: { valence: -0.1, arousal: 0.6 }        # optional
visibility: private                            # capture-consent model, see Open Questions
---
Free-form first-person thought, captured as written.
```

#### Object 3 — Dynamic per-entity ontology (the novel part)

Today an entity page has roughly fixed frontmatter. The key insight: **the salient schema differs per entity and should be allowed to grow.** Rather than predefining columns, let observed dimensions become first-class — but **typed, sourced, and confidence-weighted** so the open world stays disciplined.

```yaml
# inside an entity page's frontmatter
ontology:
  role:        { value: "advisor", confidence: high, source: meetings/2026-01-10-x.md, t: 2026-01-10 }
  reliability: { value: "high", confidence: med, source: pattern, t: 2026-01-15 }
  open_claims: { value: ["unverified figure cited 3x, no source found"], confidence: high, source: web-check, t: 2026-01-16 }
  shared_context: { value: [project-alpha, topic-beta], confidence: high }
```

Every dimension carries `confidence`, `source`, and `t` (when learned). This makes three things mechanical instead of manual:
- **No silent hardening:** a low-confidence inference can never become asserted truth — its provenance travels with it.
- **Contradiction detection:** two sources, two values for one key → flag for human review.
- **Meta-ontology discovery:** the set of dimension *keys* across all entities is itself queryable ("what kinds of things does the brain track about people?").

### How it's fed (ingestion)

1. **Auto from existing ingests (primary).** When a meeting/transcript/calendar item is ingested, an extractor emits Event(s) + proposes ontology deltas on involved entity pages. Deterministic where possible (timestamps, attendee lists), LLM-judged where it needs judgment (kind, summary, ontology dimensions). Deltas above a surprise threshold queue for confirmation; otherwise file at low confidence.
2. **Manual one-liners (always-on).** A quick-capture command files an Event/diary entry for things that never get a transcript. (Habit-formation surface — see scoping note.)
3. **Backfill.** Sweep existing `meetings/`, conversation logs, and calendar history into Events retroactively (batched, eval-gated).

### Storage / implementation — gbrain-native, no new datastore

Events and diary entries are **pages** (Markdown + frontmatter) — they get embeddings + SQL-queryable frontmatter for free. New `type:` values: `event`, `diary`. New frontmatter block: `ontology:` on entity pages. The existing `pages` table already has `frontmatter JSONB`, a `timeline TEXT` column, and `emotional_weight REAL` — so timeline assembly and affect ranking ride existing columns.

A **daily assembler** (cron / cycle phase) collects the day's Events into `life/timeline/YYYY/MM/DD.md` and updates entity `last_seen` + ontology. Idempotent.

### Proof-of-concept

A standalone assembler (no deps, ~90 LOC) already works against a real brain: it scans pages, extracts Event atoms from frontmatter, sorts, and renders a day timeline with people tags + backlinks.

```js
// life-timeline.mjs — assemble a day's timeline from page frontmatter
import fs from "node:fs";
import path from "node:path";

const day = process.argv[2];                 // YYYY-MM-DD
const brainIdx = process.argv.indexOf("--brain");
const brain = brainIdx >= 0 ? process.argv[brainIdx + 1] : "./brain";

function parseFront(md) {
  const m = md.match(/^---\n([\s\S]*?)\n---/);
  if (!m) return {};
  const fm = {};
  for (const line of m[1].split("\n")) {
    const kv = line.match(/^([a-z_]+):\s*(.*)$/i);
    if (!kv) continue;
    let [, k, v] = kv; v = v.trim();
    if (v.startsWith("[") && v.endsWith("]"))
      fm[k] = v.slice(1, -1).split(",").map(s => s.trim().replace(/^["']|["']$/g, "")).filter(Boolean);
    else fm[k] = v.replace(/^["']|["']$/g, "");
  }
  return fm;
}
const dateOf = fm => fm.date || fm.event_date || (fm.t_start || "").slice(0, 10) || null;

const events = [];
for (const dir of ["meetings", "life/events", "calls"].map(d => path.join(brain, d))) {
  if (!fs.existsSync(dir)) continue;
  for (const f of fs.readdirSync(dir).filter(f => f.endsWith(".md"))) {
    const fm = parseFront(fs.readFileSync(path.join(dir, f), "utf8"));
    if (dateOf(fm) !== day) continue;
    events.push({
      t: fm.t_start || fm.date || day,
      kind: fm.kind || fm.meeting_type || fm.type || "event",
      people: [].concat(fm.people || []),
      title: fm.title || f.replace(/\.md$/, ""),
      link: path.relative(brain, path.join(dir, f)),
    });
  }
}
events.sort((a, b) => String(a.t).localeCompare(String(b.t)));

let out = `# Timeline — ${day}\n\n`;
for (const e of events)
  out += `- **${e.t}** · _${e.kind}_${e.people.length ? " · " + e.people.join(", ") : ""}` +
         ` — ${e.title} → [page](${e.link})\n`;
console.log(events.length ? out : `_No events for ${day}._`);
```

Example output against a real brain (entities anonymized):

```
# Timeline — 2026-01-15

- **2026-01-15** · _meeting_ · person-a, person-b — Project sync → [page](meetings/2026-01-15-project-sync.md)
- **2026-01-15** · _meeting_ · person-a, person-c — Vendor call → [page](meetings/2026-01-15-vendor-call.md)
- **2026-01-15** · _meeting_ · person-d, person-e — Weekly standup → [page](meetings/2026-01-15-standup.md)
```

A subtle real bug the PoC surfaced and worth flagging for the real impl: `args.indexOf("--brain")` returns `-1` when the flag is absent, so `args[-1 + 1] === args[0]` silently captured the *date* as the brain path. Guard the flag lookup (shown above).

### Proposed retrieval surfaces

- **Temporal:** `gbrain timeline <date>` · `gbrain timeline --week-of <date>` · `gbrain last-seen <entity>` · `gbrain since <date> --kind <k>`
- **Entity rollup:** `gbrain entity <id> --chronological` → every Event + diary mention + ontology, time-ordered.
- **Introspective:** semantic over diary+events — `gbrain reflect "<query>"` (e.g. recurring patterns across months).
- **Agent context:** an agent loads the recent timeline + relevant entity ontologies to orient before acting — the exact thing missing when chronology gets fumbled.

### Scoping

Two independent workstreams:
- **A. Auto-assembly** (timeline + ontology deltas from existing ingests) — fully automatable, no behavior change required. *PoC above already demonstrates the core.*
- **B. Capture** (diary one-liners) — requires a low-friction quick-capture surface + a visibility/consent model so not every passing line becomes a logged interior thought.

### Open questions

1. Unified timeline (all `kind`s, filterable) vs. scoped streams?
2. Diary capture: passive (derive from conversation) vs. active (explicit marker) vs. both — and the consent/visibility model for passive.
3. Affect tagging on events/diary: enables "emotional arc over a month" — desirable, or over-quantifying?
4. Ontology-delta confirmation threshold: how surprising before it interrupts vs. files silently at low confidence?
5. Core gbrain capability (everyone gets a Life Chronicle) vs. opt-in module? (Leaning core engine; data stays in the operator's private brain.)

### Why it's worth building

It's the difference between a brain that *stores what it's told* and one that *models a subject over time*. The timeline makes the brain orient-able (agents stop fumbling chronology). Diary + dynamic ontology make it **introspective** — longitudinal patterns become queryable instead of re-derived. And the emergent, sourced, confidence-weighted per-entity ontology is the genuinely new primitive: most "personal memory" systems are fixed-schema CRMs. A memory where the *shape* of what-matters-about-an-entity grows from observation — with provenance — is a new retrieval primitive, for both human introspection and agent context.

title: Feature: Life Chronicle — temporal timeline + thought diary + dynamic per-entity ontology
body:
## Feature: Life Chronicle — a temporal + introspective layer for gbrain

### Summary

gbrain today is an excellent **document store with semantic + structured retrieval** (pages + typed `frontmatter JSONB` + embeddings + SQL). What it lacks is a layer that turns a pile of pages into a **model of a subject over time**.

This proposes a **Life Chronicle**: three interlocking objects built entirely on existing gbrain primitives —

1. **Daily Timeline** — auto-assembled events (`when · where · who · what`), each backlinking to the rich page that holds the depth.
2. **Thought Diary** — timestamped, low-friction interiority, backlinked to events/entities; the raw material for cross-time pattern detection.
3. **Dynamic per-entity ontology** — an open-world, sourced, confidence-weighted property bag on each entity page, where salient dimensions *emerge from observation* instead of fitting a fixed schema.

The pages remain the **depth**. The Life Chronicle is the **structure over the depth**. It is both a retrieval/introspection tool for the human and a context substrate for agents.

### Motivation

Concrete failure that motivated this: a single day's activity was captured across several rich meeting pages, but the **chronological spine** — the order of events, who was where, what came before what — was scattered across those pages. An agent reconstructing the day repeatedly got the sequence wrong (e.g. conflating a "before" event with an "after" event, or mislocating who was present at which event), because **a meeting page is great at depth and bad at sequence**. There was no object whose job is "the timeline."

Two distinct gaps fall out of that:
- Agents can't reliably answer *"what was happening the week of X?"* or *"when did the subject last interact with entity Y?"* — there's no temporal index, only a keyword/semantic one.
- There's no place for *interiority over time* — reactions, uncertainty, evolving takes — so longitudinal patterns ("every time situation Z came up, the reaction was W") must be re-derived from scratch each session instead of being queryable.

### Design

#### Object 1 — Event (timeline atom)

One Event = one page (`type: event`) with typed frontmatter + a one-clause summary that links out. Cheap; a day produces a handful.

```yaml
---
type: event
t_start: 2026-01-15T16:30:00-08:00   # ISO; date-only allowed, with t_approx: true
t_end:   2026-01-15T19:00:00-08:00   # optional
place:
  name: "Example Venue"
  area: "Example District"
  geo: [37.7587, -122.4112]          # optional
people: [person-a, person-b]          # refs to entity pages
kind: meeting                         # meeting|call|meal|solo|travel|work|... (open vocab)
mood: [focused]                       # optional, light affect tags
source: transcription                 # transcription|calendar|message|manual|inferred
confidence: high                      # high|med|low (for inferred/fuzzy timing)
links:
  - meetings/2026-01-15-example.md    # the depth page
summary: "Project sync — scope cut agreed, follow-up next week."
---
```

#### Object 2 — Diary entry (introspective atom)

```yaml
---
type: diary
t: 2026-01-16T08:10:00-08:00
people: [person-a]
events: [life/events/2026-01-15-002-example]   # what it reflects on
themes: [decision-making, uncertainty]
affect: { valence: -0.1, arousal: 0.6 }        # optional
visibility: private                            # capture-consent model, see Open Questions
---
Free-form first-person thought, captured as written.
```

#### Object 3 — Dynamic per-entity ontology (the novel part)

Today an entity page has roughly fixed frontmatter. The key insight: **the salient schema differs per entity and should be allowed to grow.** Rather than predefining columns, let observed dimensions become first-class — but **typed, sourced, and confidence-weighted** so the open world stays disciplined.

```yaml
# inside an entity page's frontmatter
ontology:
  role:        { value: "advisor", confidence: high, source: meetings/2026-01-10-x.md, t: 2026-01-10 }
  reliability: { value: "high", confidence: med, source: pattern, t: 2026-01-15 }
  open_claims: { value: ["unverified figure cited 3x, no source found"], confidence: high, source: web-check, t: 2026-01-16 }
  shared_context: { value: [project-alpha, topic-beta], confidence: high }
```

Every dimension carries `confidence`, `source`, and `t` (when learned). This makes three things mechanical instead of manual:
- **No silent hardening:** a low-confidence inference can never become asserted truth — its provenance travels with it.
- **Contradiction detection:** two sources, two values for one key → flag for human review.
- **Meta-ontology discovery:** the set of dimension *keys* across all entities is itself queryable ("what kinds of things does the brain track about people?").

### How it's fed (ingestion)

1. **Auto from existing ingests (primary).** When a meeting/transcript/calendar item is ingested, an extractor emits Event(s) + proposes ontology deltas on involved entity pages. Deterministic where possible (timestamps, attendee lists), LLM-judged where it needs judgment (kind, summary, ontology dimensions). Deltas above a surprise threshold queue for confirmation; otherwise file at low confidence.
2. **Manual one-liners (always-on).** A quick-capture command files an Event/diary entry for things that never get a transcript. (Habit-formation surface — see scoping note.)
3. **Backfill.** Sweep existing `meetings/`, conversation logs, and calendar history into Events retroactively (batched, eval-gated).

### Storage / implementation — gbrain-native, no new datastore

Events and diary entries are **pages** (Markdown + frontmatter) — they get embeddings + SQL-queryable frontmatter for free. New `type:` values: `event`, `diary`. New frontmatter block: `ontology:` on entity pages. The existing `pages` table already has `frontmatter JSONB`, a `timeline TEXT` column, and `emotional_weight REAL` — so timeline assembly and affect ranking ride existing columns.

A **daily assembler** (cron / cycle phase) collects the day's Events into `life/timeline/YYYY/MM/DD.md` and updates entity `last_seen` + ontology. Idempotent.

### Proof-of-concept

A standalone assembler (no deps, ~90 LOC) already works against a real brain: it scans pages, extracts Event atoms from frontmatter, sorts, and renders a day timeline with people tags + backlinks.

```js
// life-timeline.mjs — assemble a day's timeline from page frontmatter
import fs from "node:fs";
import path from "node:path";

const day = process.argv[2];                 // YYYY-MM-DD
const brainIdx = process.argv.indexOf("--brain");
const brain = brainIdx >= 0 ? process.argv[brainIdx + 1] : "./brain";

function parseFront(md) {
  const m = md.match(/^---\n([\s\S]*?)\n---/);
  if (!m) return {};
  const fm = {};
  for (const line of m[1].split("\n")) {
    const kv = line.match(/^([a-z_]+):\s*(.*)$/i);
    if (!kv) continue;
    let [, k, v] = kv; v = v.trim();
    if (v.startsWith("[") && v.endsWith("]"))
      fm[k] = v.slice(1, -1).split(",").map(s => s.trim().replace(/^["']|["']$/g, "")).filter(Boolean);
    else fm[k] = v.replace(/^["']|["']$/g, "");
  }
  return fm;
}
const dateOf = fm => fm.date || fm.event_date || (fm.t_start || "").slice(0, 10) || null;

const events = [];
for (const dir of ["meetings", "life/events", "calls"].map(d => path.join(brain, d))) {
  if (!fs.existsSync(dir)) continue;
  for (const f of fs.readdirSync(dir).filter(f => f.endsWith(".md"))) {
    const fm = parseFront(fs.readFileSync(path.join(dir, f), "utf8"));
    if (dateOf(fm) !== day) continue;
    events.push({
      t: fm.t_start || fm.date || day,
      kind: fm.kind || fm.meeting_type || fm.type || "event",
      people: [].concat(fm.people || []),
      title: fm.title || f.replace(/\.md$/, ""),
      link: path.relative(brain, path.join(dir, f)),
    });
  }
}
events.sort((a, b) => String(a.t).localeCompare(String(b.t)));

let out = `# Timeline — ${day}\n\n`;
for (const e of events)
  out += `- **${e.t}** · _${e.kind}_${e.people.length ? " · " + e.people.join(", ") : ""}` +
         ` — ${e.title} → [page](${e.link})\n`;
console.log(events.length ? out : `_No events for ${day}._`);
```

Example output against a real brain (entities anonymized):

```
# Timeline — 2026-01-15

- **2026-01-15** · _meeting_ · person-a, person-b — Project sync → [page](meetings/2026-01-15-project-sync.md)
- **2026-01-15** · _meeting_ · person-a, person-c — Vendor call → [page](meetings/2026-01-15-vendor-call.md)
- **2026-01-15** · _meeting_ · person-d, person-e — Weekly standup → [page](meetings/2026-01-15-standup.md)
```

A subtle real bug the PoC surfaced and worth flagging for the real impl: `args.indexOf("--brain")` returns `-1` when the flag is absent, so `args[-1 + 1] === args[0]` silently captured the *date* as the brain path. Guard the flag lookup (shown above).

### Proposed retrieval surfaces

- **Temporal:** `gbrain timeline <date>` · `gbrain timeline --week-of <date>` · `gbrain last-seen <entity>` · `gbrain since <date> --kind <k>`
- **Entity rollup:** `gbrain entity <id> --chronological` → every Event + diary mention + ontology, time-ordered.
- **Introspective:** semantic over diary+events — `gbrain reflect "<query>"` (e.g. recurring patterns across months).
- **Agent context:** an agent loads the recent timeline + relevant entity ontologies to orient before acting — the exact thing missing when chronology gets fumbled.

### Scoping

Two independent workstreams:
- **A. Auto-assembly** (timeline + ontology deltas from existing ingests) — fully automatable, no behavior change required. *PoC above already demonstrates the core.*
- **B. Capture** (diary one-liners) — requires a low-friction quick-capture surface + a visibility/consent model so not every passing line becomes a logged interior thought.

### Open questions

1. Unified timeline (all `kind`s, filterable) vs. scoped streams?
2. Diary capture: passive (derive from conversation) vs. active (explicit marker) vs. both — and the consent/visibility model for passive.
3. Affect tagging on events/diary: enables "emotional arc over a month" — desirable, or over-quantifying?
4. Ontology-delta confirmation threshold: how surprising before it interrupts vs. files silently at low confidence?
5. Core gbrain capability (everyone gets a Life Chronicle) vs. opt-in module? (Leaning core engine; data stays in the operator's private brain.)

### Why it's worth building

It's the difference between a brain that *stores what it's told* and one that *models a subject over time*. The timeline makes the brain orient-able (agents stop fumbling chronology). Diary + dynamic ontology make it **introspective** — longitudinal patterns become queryable instead of re-derived. And the emergent, sourced, confidence-weighted per-entity ontology is the genuinely new primitive: most "personal memory" systems are fixed-schema CRMs. A memory where the *shape* of what-matters-about-an-entity grows from observation — with provenance — is a new retrieval primitive, for both human introspection and agent context.

title: doctor type_proliferation failure dominates overall health despite operationally healthy brain
body:
## Summary

`gbrain doctor` can report a hard `type_proliferation` failure that drives the overall health score down even when the brain is operationally healthy according to `gbrain health` and the operational doctor categories.

Observed on a real private ops brain after scout/report workflows created many domain-specific frontmatter `type:` values.

## Observed output

`gbrain health`:

```text
Health score: 8/10
Embed coverage: 100.0%
Missing embeddings: 0
Stale pages: 42
Link coverage (entities): 79.3%
Timeline coverage (entities): 90.2%
```

`gbrain stats`:

```text
Pages: 1419
Chunks: 2909
Embedded: 2909
Links: 448
Tags: 465
Timeline: 296
```

`gbrain doctor` tail:

```text
[WARN] pack_upgrade_available: Active pack: gbrain-base@1.0.0+7bd490ab. Successor available: gbrain-base-v2@1.0.0+b9bebaa4. Preview: `gbrain onboard --check --explain`
[FAIL] type_proliferation: 83 distinct page types (pack declares 25). Run `gbrain onboard --check --explain` to preview a pack upgrade or define a custom pack with mapping_rules.

Brain checks:  95/100  (category penalty)
Skill checks:  90/100
Ops checks:    100/100
Meta checks:   65/100
Weighted brain score: [WARN] Brain score 57/100 (embed 35/35, links 8/25, timeline 1/15, orphans 3/15, dead-links 10/10)

Overall health score: 50/100. Failed checks found.
```

## Why this is confusing

Operationally the brain is healthy:

- embeddings complete;
- sync succeeds;
- no stale chunks;
- ops checks 100/100;
- brain checks 95/100;
- `gbrain health` reports 8/10.

But `gbrain doctor` returns an overall 50/100 with `Failed checks found`, dominated by schema/meta debt.

For agent/heartbeat workflows this is noisy: the operator sees a failure score even though the actionable state is “schema taxonomy needs maintenance, not runtime incident.”

## Expected behavior

One of these would make the failure easier to operate:

1. classify `type_proliferation` as a remediation/debt warning unless it breaks routing/extraction; or
2. split `overall health` into `operational_health` vs `schema_taxonomy_health`; or
3. have doctor output a clear line like:

```text
Operational status: OK; schema taxonomy debt: FAIL(type_proliferation)
```

## Suggested remediation path

`gbrain onboard --check --explain` should ideally propose one of:

- upgrade to `gbrain-base-v2` if available and safe;
- generate mapping_rules for observed type aliases;
- suggest a custom schema pack for domain-specific report/case/scout page types.

## Notes

This report is intentionally anonymized from a private operational brain. Exact page slugs and organization-specific type names are omitted.

title: fix(import): decode UTF-16 text files instead of mangling them into NUL bytes
body:
## Problem

`importFile()` read every file with `readFileSync(path, 'utf-8')`. UTF-16 sources — the norm for MetaTrader MQL files and common for Windows-authored notes — decode under UTF-8 into strings riddled with `U+0000`. Postgres then rejects the insert with `invalid byte sequence for encoding "UTF8": 0x00`, which aborts the **entire** sync (every file in the batch fails the checkpoint, `last_commit` never advances).

This is encoding-general, not language-specific — any UTF-16 markdown or code file hits it.

## Fix

Add `readTextFileUtf8()` / `decodeTextBuffer()` and route the single import read boundary through it:

- **BOM-driven** decoding when a BOM is present (UTF-16 LE/BE, UTF-8 BOM stripped).
- **No-BOM UTF-16 heuristic**: valid UTF-8 text never contains a `NUL` byte, so a meaningful run of them signals UTF-16; byte-parity of the NULs picks the endianness. This covers MetaTrader's common BOM-less export shape.
- **Plain UTF-8 is returned unchanged** — zero behaviour change for the overwhelmingly common case.

## Tests

- `test/import-utf16.test.ts` — UTF-16 LE/BE with BOM, BOM-less UTF-16 LE, plain UTF-8, and UTF-8-with-BOM, all asserting clean UTF-8 out with no residual `NUL`.
- Verified end-to-end through the real `sync --strategy code` → DB path: a UTF-16 file that previously failed with the `0x00` error now imports cleanly.

Complements the MQL code-intelligence work (#2299): MetaTrader's MQL files are predominantly UTF-16, so this is what lets a real MQL corpus ingest at all.

*Authored with AI assistance (Claude) under the contributor's direction.*

title: v0.42.55.0 fix(security): dotfile/skills/slug confinement + DCR consent default + schema-lint migration (#418 #419 #245 #1353 #1647 #171 #1385)
body:
## Security-hardening wave (v0.42.55.0)

A focused security pass closing several still-open, community-reported gaps. Fresh installs were already covered; existing brains are brought to the same bar automatically on upgrade. Every claim was verified against current `master` before landing — several "open security PRs" turned out already-fixed upstream and are **not** in this wave (see "Closed as superseded" below).

Atomic, bisect-friendly commits separate the pure code-path hardening from the schema migration (the eng review's blast-radius split, shipped as one PR per the repo's bisect-commits convention).

### What's in it

**Code-path hardening (no migration):**
- **#418 (@garagon)** — `.gbrain-source` / `.gbrain-mount` walk-up dotfiles are `lstat` trust-gated (owned-by-you-or-root, non-symlink, non-world-writable; fail-closed). Registered-path routing realpaths both sides so a symlinked CWD can't misattribute source/brain. Extended to the brain axis, not just source.
- **#419 (@garagon)** — every skills-dir resolution tier (env, `cwd_walk_up`, `repo_root`, `cwd_skills`, `install_path`) routes through realpath containment, so a symlinked `workspace/skills` can't escape the declared workspace.
- **#245 (@aliceagent)** — large-file transcription uses `execFileSync` arg-arrays + `fs.rmSync` (no shell); a media path with shell metacharacters is never parsed by a shell.
- **slug write boundary** — `validateSlug` rejects control bytes, bidi/RTL overrides, backslashes, and URL-encoded separators at the shared `putPage`/`updateSlug` chokepoint; write-through confirms the file path stays inside the source tree. Ordinary/CJK slugs unaffected.
- **#1353** — Dynamic Client Registration defaults self-registered clients to `authorization_code` (consent-bearing) instead of `client_credentials`; `--enable-dcr-insecure` is the explicit opt-in; a startup WARNING prints whenever DCR is open.

**Schema-lint migration v120 (both engines):**
- **#1647** — `page_links` view runs with `security_invoker` on Postgres (honors the caller's RLS).
- **#1647 / #171** — gbrain-owned trigger/event functions pin `SET search_path` (via `ALTER FUNCTION IF EXISTS`, body untouched — safe for the load-bearing `auto_enable_rls`). Fresh-install definitions are born-correct; `scripts/check-search-path.sh` is a new CI guard wired into `verify`.
- **#1385** — the RLS preflight in the historical migration gates now recognizes superuser + inherited-role BYPASSRLS, so a superuser-connected fresh install no longer aborts.

### Verification
- `bun run verify`: **31/31** green (incl. the new `check:search-path` guard + typecheck).
- Security + blast-radius suites on the merged tree: **all green** (path-confine 35, oauth 95 incl. 3 new DCR, transcription-injection, migrate + schema-bootstrap 170, migration-v120 proconfig/idempotency, slug/page/import/write-through 251, facts/conversation isolation 373).
- Postgres-only assertions (`security_invoker`, function `proconfig`) added to the bootstrap E2E; the PGLite path is exercised by `test/migration-v120.test.ts`.
- The full-at-once `bun test` shows timeout flakes in unrelated facts/conversation files under concurrent PGLite spin-up; those pass in isolation and CI runs sharded.

### Closed as superseded (verified already-fixed in master — no code here)
#983 (CORS preflight, v0.41.3), #1371/#2200/#1790 (source-scope, #1999), #2027/#2072 (legacy-token grant, #2128), #1705/#1526 (reclone, #1881), #842/#1243 (git-SSRF flags, #1053), #930, #960, #70, #616.

### Deferred follow-ups (separate vehicles)
- **CI/security-process track**: Semgrep SAST + OSV-Scanner + npm `"private"` + enable Private Vulnerability Reporting.
- A `doctor` `proconfig` probe (defense-in-depth; the migration + CI guard already cover regression).
- Close the superseded issues above with credit; delete the dead `enrichment-service.ts`; expand the federated by-slug P1 TODO (`takes_search`/`resolve_slugs`/`code_def`).

title: v0.42.57.0 fix(pglite): incident — never steal a live data-dir lock + corrupted-store recovery hint (#2348)
body:
## Incident: PGLite brain corruption after `gbrain dream`

#2348 — after `gbrain dream`'s sync phase, subsequent calls failed with `relation "content_chunks" does not exist` / 58P01 `internal_load_library`; brain locked, only wipe+restore recovered. **Reproduced and root-caused.**

### Root cause
`src/core/pglite-lock.ts` stole the data-dir lock from a holder whose 30s heartbeat had lapsed past a grace window. But the heartbeat runs on the JS event loop, which is **blocked during long synchronous WASM imports/CHECKPOINTs** — so a genuinely working `dream`/`embed` looked stale while fully alive. PGLite/WASM is strictly single-writer; reaping a live holder let a second OS process open the same data dir and corrupt the catalog + pgvector extension state. A subagent reproduced the exact corruption deterministically (two OS processes on one data dir → `type "vector" does not exist`, catalog gutted; `rm postmaster.pid`/`.gbrain-lock` does not recover).

### Fix
- **Never steal a live holder** (`pglite-lock.ts`): reap only a *dead* PID. A wedged-but-alive or PID-reused holder makes the acquire time out with a message naming the PID, rather than risk corruption. Removes the now-meaningless `GBRAIN_PGLITE_LOCK_STEAL_GRACE_SECONDS` knob. Inverts the prior test that asserted the corruption behavior.
- **Recovery hint for already-corrupted stores** (`pglite-engine.ts`): `classifyPgliteInitError` gains a `corrupt` verdict (58P01 / `internal_load_library` / vector/content_chunks missing — beats the generic wasm-runtime match) pointing at `gbrain reinit-pglite` / backup restore, instead of the wrong macOS-WASM hint.

### Tests
`test/pglite-lock.test.ts` (live-stale holder NOT stolen), `test/pglite-init-classifier.test.ts` (corrupt verdict + precedence + recovery message). Dependent lock/cycle/disconnect suites green. Typecheck clean.

## Also in this incident: #2296 (process leak) — closed as fixed-on-master
Root-caused: NOT a `serve` spawn. The reporter (v0.28.1) hit a one-shot command that wouldn't exit (open pool / dangling timer); under a headless driver it looked like a leaked process. Already fixed on master by #1633 (clearInterval+unref) and #2084 (`cli-force-exit`/`flushThenExit`). **Verified live**: `embed`/`sync` exit cleanly against a temp brain with zero surviving children. Closed #2296 with upgrade guidance (no code change).

## Deferred to follow-up (noted, not built)
Automatic PID-reuse detection (start-time/boot-id token), a kernel `flock` second-open guard, and a full `gbrain recover` command. The steal-prevention + recovery hint close the incident; these are hardening.

## Merge order / version
Takes **v0.42.57.0** — re-bumped twice as master advanced (#2399 took 0.42.55.0, #2533 took 0.42.56.0); branch is merged up to current master and MERGEABLE. The silent-failure WAVE (#2398) is independent and re-bumps on its own.

title: fix(sync): crash-safe renames loop — record per-file failures instead of throwing
body:
## What

The renames loop in `performSyncInner` reimports each renamed file via `importFile()` with **no `try/catch`** — unlike the deletes loop and the adds/mods loop, which both record per-file failures to `failedFiles`. This wraps the renames reimport to match those loops.

## Why

`importFile()` returns a status, but it still **throws** on several paths — content sanity-block (`ContentSanityBlockError`), duplicate-slug, and missing-link endpoints. In the renames loop an uncaught throw propagates all the way out and **crashes the entire sync mid-run**, freezing the checkpoint and defeating `--skip-failed`. A `skipped`-with-error result was also silently dropped (never recorded to `failedFiles`).

I hit this in the wild on a tree-wide rename — a `shared/ → system/` vault reorg of ~10,857 renames. One malformed-YAML renamed file threw and killed incremental sync at rename ~4,900/10,857, with `--skip-failed` set. The deletes/adds loops would have recorded-and-skipped it; the renames loop crashed.

(Note: the related `maxBuffer` ENOBUFS fix in `git()` and the `failedFiles` hoist are already on `master` — this PR is only the remaining renames-loop gap.)

## Change

Wrap the renames `importFile()` call in `try/catch`, pushing both the thrown error and the `skipped`-with-error case to `failedFiles` — identical to the existing deletes/adds pattern. `sync.ts` only, +16/-3, no behavior change on the happy path.

title: ops/ hardcoded in PRUNE_DIR_NAMES: sync silently deletes ops/* pages and never imports ops/* files
body:
# Bug: `ops/` directory is hardcoded in `PRUNE_DIR_NAMES`, so sync silently deletes any `ops/*` page and never imports `ops/*` files

**gbrain version:** 0.41.14.0
**Component:** `src/core/sync.ts` (and the delete path in `src/commands/sync.ts`)
**Severity:** High — silent loss of pages from the brain DB (markdown source files are unaffected, but the pages vanish and can never be re-synced).

## Summary

`PRUNE_DIR_NAMES` in `src/core/sync.ts` includes the literal string **`'ops'`** alongside
`'node_modules'` and `'.raw'`. `classifySync()` treats **any path containing an `ops`
segment** as `'pruned-dir'`, so:

- `isSyncable('ops/anything.md')` returns `false` → `collectSyncableFiles` / `runImport` /
  `performFullSync` **never treat `ops/*` files as import candidates** (even `gbrain sync --full`
  reports `imported=0` for them).
- A **modified** `ops/*` file falls into the `unsyncableModified` delete loop in
  `commands/sync.ts`. Its `unsyncableReason()` is `'pruned-dir'` (not `'metafile'`), so the
  delete-skip guard does **not** fire, and the page is **deleted** ("Deleted un-syncable page").

Net effect: **any page under a directory named `ops` is deleted on every sync and can never be
(re)imported.** This includes pages created via `gbrain put` with an `ops/...` slug — they are
silently destroyed by the next `gbrain sync` or `gbrain dream`.

Because `PRUNE_DIR_NAMES` matches a **single path segment basename at any depth**, the very
common directory name `ops/` (operations notes, runbooks, etc.) is unusable.

## Reproduction

```sh
# 1) A put-created ops page is deleted on the next sync:
echo -e "---\ntype: note\ntitle: t\ncreated: '2026-01-01'\n---\nhello" > /tmp/x.md
gbrain put ops/x < /tmp/x.md
gbrain list | grep ops/x          # present
gbrain sync                       # -> "Deleted un-syncable page: ops/x"
gbrain list | grep ops/x          # gone

# 2) A committed ops/*.md file is never imported:
mkdir -p <brain-repo>/ops && cp /tmp/x.md <brain-repo>/ops/x.md
git -C <brain-repo> add ops/x.md && git -C <brain-repo> commit -m x
gbrain sync                       # ops/x NOT imported
gbrain sync --full                # imported=0 for ops/* (skipped as "pruned-dir", not "unchanged")
```

Pages under other directories (e.g. `regulatory/`, `audits/`) sync normally — they differ only
in that their paths contain no `ops` segment.

## Expected behavior

`ops/` is an ordinary content directory and should sync, import, update, and delete like any
other path. Nothing about the name `ops` implies it's internal/generated.

## Root cause

`PRUNE_DIR_NAMES` is intended to skip generated/internal directories (`node_modules`, `.raw`),
but `'ops'` was added to it. Matching it as a bare segment name prunes every user `ops/`
directory at any depth.

## Suggested fix

1. **Remove `'ops'` from `PRUNE_DIR_NAMES`.** (The one-line fix; resolves the issue entirely.)
2. If there is a legitimate internal `ops` location to exclude, scope it precisely instead of
   pruning the bare segment everywhere — e.g. match a full relative path (`.gbrain/ops`) or a
   reserved-prefix convention (`_ops/`), not any directory literally named `ops`.
3. Hardening: when the delete path encounters a `'pruned-dir'` reason for a file that **exists in
   the repo working tree**, prefer skipping the delete (or importing) over deleting — silent
   deletion of a present, tracked file is surprising and `gbrain doctor` does not surface it.

## Workaround (until fixed)

Remove the `'ops'` entry from `PRUNE_DIR_NAMES` in
`~/.bun/install/global/node_modules/gbrain/src/core/sync.ts` (the bin runs `src/cli.ts` directly
via bun, so no rebuild is needed). Note: `gbrain upgrade` overwrites the package and re-adds the
entry, re-breaking it — must be re-applied after every upgrade, and `gbrain doctor` won't flag it.

## Validation of the fix

After removing `'ops'`: put→sync keeps the page (survives repeated syncs); a committed `ops/*.md`
imports natively (`+1 added`); editing an `ops/*` note updates it (`~N modified`, not deleted); a
real `git rm` still deletes the page correctly; a full `gbrain dream` completes (exit 0) with the
`ops/*` pages intact; `regulatory/` and `audits/` unaffected.

title: doctor pack checks can report a different active schema pack than gbrain schema active
body:
## Summary

After activating a custom schema pack, `gbrain schema active` reported the expected active pack and page type count, while `gbrain doctor` still reported pack-related findings using the previous `gbrain-base` identity and type count. This suggests the doctor checks for `pack_upgrade_available` and `type_proliferation` are resolving schema pack state through a path that can drift from the authoritative active-pack resolver.

The result is confusing operator guidance: one command says the configured pack is active, while doctor findings appear to be computed against a stale or different pack.

## Reproduction steps

1. Create or install a non-default schema pack.
2. Run `gbrain schema use <pack-name>`.
3. Run `gbrain schema active`.
4. Run `gbrain doctor`.
5. Compare the pack name and declared type count reported by the doctor pack checks with the output from `schema active`.

## Expected behavior

Doctor pack checks should use the same active schema pack resolver as `gbrain schema active`.

## Actual behavior

In a live 0.42.52.0 setup, `schema active` reported the custom active pack with 21 page types, while `doctor` still reported `gbrain-base@1.0.0` and an older declared type count.

## Proposed fix / approach

Route the doctor pack checks through the same resolver used by `gbrain schema active`, or centralize the active-pack resolution so CLI inspection and doctor diagnostics cannot diverge.

## Context

Observed on gbrain 0.42.52.0 during a schema-pack maintenance session on 2026-06-23. The maintenance note records that `gbrain schema active` correctly showed the custom `house` pack with 21 page types, while `doctor` still reported the old `gbrain-base@1.0.0` pack and its old declared type count. The issue is based on that observed command divergence rather than a single obvious source line.

title: dream.synthesize and patterns write to the hardcoded wiki/ namespace with no config override
body:
## Summary

`dream.synthesize` and `patterns` hardcode `wiki/` output paths in both prompt text and filing rules. That works for brains that use the default `wiki/` layout, but it breaks the dream pipeline for installations whose canonical content root is different. Generated pages land under a namespace the brain does not use, which means synthesis output has to be moved or patched after the fact before it fits the rest of the content model.

The hardcoded namespace appears in three places:

1. `src/core/cycle/synthesize.ts`
2. `src/core/cycle/patterns.ts`
3. `skills/_brain-filing-rules.json`

## Reproduction steps

1. Configure a brain that uses a top-level content namespace other than `wiki/`.
2. Run `dream synthesize` or the related patterns phase.
3. Inspect generated slugs and filing-rule enforcement.
4. Observe that generated paths still target `wiki/...`.

## Expected behavior

The dream output root should be configurable, with `wiki/` retained as the backward-compatible default. Generated pages should land inside the brain's configured content namespace.

## Actual behavior

The prompt templates and enforced allow-list hardcode `wiki/...` paths, so a non-`wiki/` brain receives output in the wrong namespace.

## Proposed fix / approach

Add a config key such as `dream.synthesize.output_root`, defaulting to `wiki/`. Use that value consistently in:

1. Reflection slug templates.
2. Original-idea slug templates.
3. Pattern reflection lookup.
4. Pattern output slug instructions.
5. Filing-rule allow-list generation or loading.

## Context

Verified against current upstream source on 2026-06-25. Current source still contains `wiki/personal/reflections`, `wiki/originals`, and `wiki/personal/patterns` in the dream pipeline.

title: Concept/landscape queries silently default to keyword search instead of hybrid (`query`) — no affordance steers agents to semantic retrieval
body:
## Summary

gbrain exposes two retrieval commands as peers:

- `search <query>` — keyword search (tsvector)
- `query <question>` / `ask` — hybrid search (RRF + expansion, embeddings)

For an agent driving gbrain, nothing in the command surface or docs signals *which* to use for *which kind* of question. The result: agents reach for keyword search by default (it's the first-listed, simplest mental model), and only escalate to hybrid `query` when keyword "comes back thin." That fallback heuristic is the bug.

## The failure mode

A keyword pass for a fuzzy *concept* request ("all the X that do Y", "the landscape of Z", "anything matching <abstract category>") returns *some* results — so it never looks "thin," so the hybrid fallback never fires. But keyword recall only covers documents that happen to use the exact tokens the agent guessed. Anything described in synonym/outcome terms is silently omitted. The agent sees a populated result set and treats "got results" as "got the complete answer."

Concrete recall failure we hit: a record whose text contained a two-word spelling (`"off shore"`) was missed by a `%offshore%` keyword filter (one word). A single whitespace dropped a real, relevant hit. Hybrid/semantic retrieval surfaced it immediately. This generalizes: keyword cannot fail loudly, so completeness bugs are invisible at the call site.

## Why this is a gbrain-level issue (not just a caller mistake)

The tooling actively trains the wrong default:

1. **`search` is listed first** and reads as the primary verb; `query` reads as an advanced/optional alternative.
2. **No routing guidance** ships with either command. Neither help text says "use hybrid for concept/landscape/exhaustive-set questions; use keyword for known exact tokens / structured fields."
3. **The fallback framing is backwards.** The implicit rule agents inherit is "keyword first, semantic if thin." For concept questions the correct rule is the inverse: **semantic-first for recall completeness, keyword as a complementary precision/known-token pass.** A nonzero keyword count must NOT be treated as a completeness signal.

## Requested changes

1. **Help-text routing hints** on both `search` and `query`: one line each stating when each wins (keyword = exact known token / structured field / historical exact-match; hybrid = concept, synonym, landscape, "all/every/anything matching", recent-recall).
2. **A `--why`/decision note or a single recommended entry point** (e.g. make `query` the documented default for natural-language questions, and position `search` as the exact-token tool). Reduce the chance an agent picks keyword for a concept question.
3. **Docs:** add an explicit "choosing a retrieval mode" section, including the anti-pattern: *"a populated keyword result set is not proof of completeness."*
4. **Optional but ideal:** a heuristic in the query path that detects concept-shaped natural-language input (no exact identifiers, fuzzy quantifier like "all/every/anything/landscape") and either auto-runs hybrid or emits a hint suggesting `query` over `search`.

## Acceptance

- `search --help` and `query --help` each state when to use them and when not to.
- Docs contain a retrieval-mode decision guide + the "keyword count != completeness" anti-pattern.
- (If implemented) concept-shaped input to `search` surfaces a suggestion to use hybrid `query`.

## Impact

This is a silent-recall-loss class bug: the system returns plausible-but-incomplete answers for exactly the high-value question type (landscape/sector/exhaustive-set queries) and gives no signal that anything was missed.

title: Write-through content stays DB-only and is silently deleted by `sync --full` (3 compounding durability bugs)
body:
## Summary

On a brain that uses the markdown write-through path (`sync.repo_path`), **write-through content never reaches git, and `sync --full` then silently deletes it.** Three compounding issues turn "DB-only content" (which is unavoidable given #1/#2) into permanent data loss. We hit this in production: a `sync --full` delete-reconcile soft-deleted ~2,780 genuine pages (years of daily digests, call transcripts, a long-form strategy doc, a real contact page) whose only fault was that their markdown had never been committed to git.

Versions: engine `0.42.52`, durability scaffolding installed via `gbrain sources harden` (post-commit hook + `scripts/brain-commit-push.sh` + 30-min pull cron).

## 1. Write-through is never committed/pushed

`put_page` / `capture` and the enrichment cycle write `.md` into the `sync.repo_path` clone (write-through), but nothing commits or pushes it:

- `gbrain sources harden` (verified via `--dry-run`) installs the post-commit hook, the `brain-commit-push.sh` helper, the durability RESOLVER rules, and the pull cron, and it pulls — but it does **not** itself commit pending write-through. Output on a dirty tree: `[pull] skipped: working tree dirty — pull skipped (in-progress edits preserved)`. No commit/push step.
- The post-commit hook is documented as "best-effort background auto-push," but it only fires **after a commit** — and write-through never makes one.
- Nothing invokes `brain-commit-push.sh` for enrichment write-through (modified `people/*.md`, `companies/*.md`, daily/email digests).

**Result:** write-through `.md` accumulates uncommitted in the clone indefinitely (we found 64 such files, mtimes days after their last commit) and never reaches the remote. There's a pull cron but no push trigger.

**Repro:** run an enrichment/dream cycle, then `git -C <clone> status --porcelain '*.md'` → modified pages, uncommitted, never pushed.

## 2. `brain-commit-push.sh` pulls before staging → fails on any modified file

The shipped helper does `git fetch` + `git pull --rebase` **before** `git add -- "$@"`. On any dirty tree (i.e. a modified/enriched page — exactly the write-through case) the rebase aborts:

```
error: cannot pull with rebase: You have unstaged changes.
error: please commit or stash them.
rebase conflict: manual attention needed   # exit 3
```

So even when the helper *is* invoked, it can only commit **untracked-new** files (which don't block a rebase), never **modifications**. Enrichment write-through (which modifies existing pages) can never be pushed by it.

**Fix:** stage → commit → `pull --rebase` → push (commit before pull), which is the correct order for "I have local changes and the remote may have advanced." (We verified this ordering works where the as-shipped order fails.)

## 3. `sync --full` delete-reconcile deletes DB-only pages without re-exporting them

Because of #1 and #2, a brain inevitably accumulates genuine DB-only pages. The `sync --full` delete-reconcile soft-deletes **any** DB page whose `source_path` file is absent from the clone — including these genuine DB-only pages — without first materializing them to git. There's no "is this content only in the DB?" guard before the destructive phase.

In our case this soft-deleted ~2,780 genuine pages in one pass. A verification that only checked "is the deleted page absent from the git clone?" reported the reconcile as clean — but "absent from git" is precisely the symptom of #1, not evidence the content is disposable.

**Suggested fixes (any one helps):**
- Before the destructive phase, export DB-only pages (content present, no clone file) to the clone so they're git-backed, then reconcile.
- Skip-not-delete pages whose content exists only in the DB (treat "missing from git but present in DB" as "needs export," not "delete").
- Gate the deletion behind an explicit `--allow-db-only-deletion` flag so it can't happen silently.

## Why these compound

#1 guarantees DB-only content exists. #2 means even a wired caller can't fix it for modified pages. #3 then deletes that content on the next full sync, and the natural "is it in git?" sanity check rubber-stamps the deletion. Individually each is a paper cut; together they're silent data loss on the system-of-record path.

title: Fork entry 10 runtime relink
ModelMessage[] schema rejects Date in tool-result output.value (Postgres timestamps crash multi-tool loops)
body:
Summary: Any multi-tool rollout or subagent loop that calls a brain tool returning Postgres timestamp columns (brain_list_pages, brain_query, etc.) crashes AI SDK v6 validation with AI_InvalidPromptError: The messages do not match the ModelMessage[] schema.
Repro:

Run gbrain skillopt <skill> (or any subagent loop) where a tool returns rows with updated_at/created_at.
The tool loop calls gateway.chat() to continue; toModelMessages() converts the tool-result message.
AI SDK v6 validates and throws the schema error the moment a tool result is included.

Root cause: toModelMessages() (src/core/ai/gateway.ts, the json branch of the tool-result mapping) emits { type: 'json', value: b.output }. node-postgres auto-deserializes timestamp columns into JavaScript Date instances. Zod's jsonValueSchema accepts only null | string | number | boolean | record | array — not Date — so the entire message tree is rejected. The failing path resolves to e.g. messages[N].content[1].output.value[0].updated_at: expected string, received Date.
Fix (one line):
ts// before
: { type: 'json', value: (b.output ?? null) }
// after
: { type: 'json', value: JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(b.output ?? null)) }
JSON.stringify invokes Date.prototype.toJSON() → ISO string; other non-JSON values get serialized too. Verified: rollout success rate went 1/5 → 5/5 on a real skill optimization.
File: src/core/ai/gateway.ts — the json branch of toModelMessages()'s tool-result mapping.

title: marked.lexer transient-memory amplification OOMs bulk import on fence-less pages
body:
## Summary

`extractFencedChunks()` in `src/core/import-file.ts` runs `marked.lexer()` on **every** page body to pull out fenced code blocks. `marked.lexer` allocates transient memory proportional to the page size on every call, even for pages that contain no code fence at all. On large table- or document-heavy pages this transient spike is large enough that, during a bulk `import`/`sync` on an already-loaded brain, it can OOM the worker. The `try/catch` around the lexer cannot rescue this — an OOM is process death, not a throwable error.

## Reproduction

A ~2 MB markdown table (the shape produced when a spreadsheet/doc is converted to a wiki page) — **no code fence** — drives `marked.lexer` to ~110 MB of transient heap to produce a handful of tokens:

```js
// repro.mjs — run from repo root: node --max-old-space-size=80 repro.mjs
import { marked } from 'marked';
const rows = 12000, cols = 16;
const header = '| ' + Array.from({length: cols}, (_, i) => 'col' + i).join(' | ') + ' |';
const sep    = '| ' + Array.from({length: cols}, () => '---').join(' | ') + ' |';
const body   = Array.from({length: rows}, (_, r) =>
  '| ' + Array.from({length: cols}, (_, c) => 'v' + r + '_' + c).join(' | ') + ' |').join('\n');
const md = '# Overview\n\n' + header + '\n' + sep + '\n' + body + '\n';  // NO ``` fence
marked.lexer(md);                                                       // <-- spikes here
```

| heap cap | result |
|---|---|
| `--max-old-space-size=512` | OK, ~110 MB heap for 3 tokens (≈60× input amplification) |
| `--max-old-space-size=80`  | **FATAL — JS heap out of memory** inside `marked.lexer` |

In a fresh process with plenty of headroom no single page OOMs; the failure appears when free heap drops below the per-page transient need (e.g. the worker is already holding a large brain's chunk/embedding working set). That matches the observed field failure: it surfaced only once the brain was substantially full, not on a cold import.

## Why this is wasteful as well as risky

On a representative brain, **~99% of importable pages contain no code fence**, so `marked.lexer` is pure wasted work on them — it can never yield a `fenced_code` chunk. The largest no-fence pages are exactly the ones with the biggest transient spike (converted tables/docs).

## Proposed fix

Skip the lexer entirely when the body has no fence marker:

```ts
// in extractFencedChunks(), before marked.lexer(...)
if (!/(^|\n)[ \t]{0,3}(```|~~~)/.test(markdown)) return out;
```

- Zero correctness cost: a page with no ``` / `~~~` fence cannot produce a fenced chunk.
- Must match **both** ` ``` ` and `~~~`, or tilde-fenced code extraction regresses.

### Scope / limitation (intentionally honest)

This removes the transient-allocation surface for the common (fence-less) case, which is what causes the field OOM. It does **not** make `marked.lexer` safe for pages that *do* contain a fence — a structurally pathological fenced page (e.g. very deeply nested lists) can still OOM. A complete hardening would additionally cap input size / nesting before lexing. Filing the fence-less skip first because it is zero-risk and covers the observed incident; happy to follow up with the input cap.

## Environment

- `marked` ^18.0.0
- Surfaced during `gbrain import`/`sync` of a large brain under memory pressure.

title: v0.42.27.0 fix(ai-gateway): fix silent no-op in Anthropic prompt caching; wire OpenAI prompt_cache_key
body:
## What this fixes

Anthropic prompt caching in the chat gateway was a **silent no-op**. `chat()` set `cache_control` on the top-level `generateText` call options, but `@ai-sdk/anthropic` reads cache markers only from each system-message's / tool's own `providerOptions` — and `ai` core converts a bare `system:` string into a system message with **no** `providerOptions`. So every `cacheSystem:true` caller (`enrich`, page summaries, skillopt, the gateway tool loop) wrote **zero** cache breakpoints while the usage telemetry kept reading 0 cache tokens — nothing looked broken, but no caching happened.

Verified against the installed SDKs: `@ai-sdk/anthropic` 3.0.74 (`validator.getCacheControl(providerOptions, …)` is per-message/per-tool), `ai` 6.0.174 (`standardizePrompt` drops a string system's providerOptions). The SDK's own `SystemModelMessage` docs say this is the supported path for caching.

## Changes

`src/core/ai/gateway.ts`:
- **`buildChatCacheArgs()`** (new, pure, exported for tests) — places markers where the provider reads them: the system prompt as a `SystemModelMessage` carrying `providerOptions`, plus `cache_control` on the **last tool def** (Anthropic caches the whole tools→system prefix up to the marked block). Restores the documented `ChatOpts.cacheSystem` contract ("cache system prompt + last tool def"). Mirrors the already-correct native subagent path.
- **`openAIPromptCacheKey()` + `ChatOpts.cacheKey`** (new) — sets `providerOptions.openai.promptCacheKey` (`prompt_cache_key`) for **native-openai only**, derived from `sha256(system + sorted tool names)`. OpenAI caches prefixes automatically; the stable key keeps shared-prefix requests on the same engine to raise the hit rate. Tool order does not change the key; explicit `cacheKey` overrides.
- Removed the dead top-level `providerOptions.anthropic.cacheControl` (it was the no-op). Added imports: `type SystemModelMessage` from `ai`, `createHash` from `node:crypto`.

`test/gateway-prompt-cache.test.ts` (new) — 10 cases pinning marker placement + routing-key derivation. The load-bearing assertion (`typeof system).not.toBe('string')` when caching is on) reproduces the exact failure mode so it can't silently regress.

## Testing

- New suite: 10 pass / 0 fail
- Adjacent gateway tests (`gateway-model-messages`, `facts-meta-cache`, `think-gateway-adapter`): 28 pass / 0 fail
- `bun run typecheck`: 0 errors
- Version audit: VERSION / package.json / CHANGELOG all at `0.42.27.0`

## How to confirm the savings end-to-end

The unit tests pin placement; the definitive proof is runtime telemetry (already captured in `ChatResult.usage`): run a `cacheSystem:true` caller (e.g. `gbrain enrich`) twice with the same system prompt and check `cache_read_tokens` goes 0 → non-zero on the second call. For OpenAI, watch `providerMetadata.openai` cached-token counts climb across same-system calls.

## Notes

- Gemini and other providers are unchanged (implicit caching only — the right call).
- The full multi-agent pre-landing review army was not run; this change is small, SDK-source-verified, and unit-pinned.
